section.title: Brendan Burns: Kubernetes Strategy, Open Source, and Convincing Management
section.deck: Burns explains how Kubernetes was pitched inside Google, why it was open sourced and governed independently, and what the team learned about scale and career choices.

blocks.text: Burns describes Kubernetes as a prototype built by Burns, Craig, and Joe that then had to be argued for inside Google. In Burns's view, a running system persuades more than a strategy document. Open source was the realistic route once other companies were building similar tools, and written governance kept any single company from controlling the roadmap. Editorial framing: the rounds follow the interview order, from business case to build, architecture, governance, scale and career.
blocks.heading: Burns's view: a running prototype persuades more than a strategy document

blocks.question: What would Burns have told Google's leadership about the impact of building Kubernetes for the industry?
answer: Burns says the hardest early task was persuading people inside Google, though the team was clear on the goal. Burns gave three arguments. The first drew on MapReduce and the big data wave. Google had written the original white paper, but Hadoop re-implemented the ideas as an open source project, and Google got no credit.

The second argument was about containers. Burns says reliable software needs systems that act like autopilots for applications. The third was open source, which Burns calls the most interesting part. People accepted that the system should be built, then asked why it should not stay on Google's own platform.

followups.question: Why would it not work to keep Kubernetes only on Google's platform?
answer: Burns says many people were on other clouds or on premises, and an exclusive product would shut them out. They would build an alternative. Burns compares this with Linux, which won because it could run anywhere. Most people were not on the leading platform, and Google Cloud was not the leader.

Burns's answer is to build for everyone, and make the system strongest on Google's platform. Burns also says that if nearly everything else was open, a closed project would need to be so differentiated that people wanted it anyway.
followups.speaker: Brendan Burns

followups.question: Was the idea to take market share from AWS, so developers would migrate to GCP?
answer: Burns describes AWS as dominant and first, and GCP as up and coming. Burns agrees the aim was attention, but adds that copying an existing model, such as virtual machines, is hard to sell. Creating a new field where Google was the thought leader gave it a voice, even among people who did not use its platform.
Burns says the strategy did not fully work, because GCP was still third. Burns would not call it a failure. Kubernetes consolidated across the cloud market and is now a utility everywhere.
followups.speaker: Brendan Burns

followups.question: Did leadership understand the visibility benefits when they agreed to the project?
answer: Burns says the team explicitly wanted to be front and center in thought leadership. That value is hard to quantify. The effort was cheap, with about eight or nine engineers.

Burns calls the separate Kubernetes brand a blessing and a curse. It gave the team freedom to fail without damaging Google Cloud's reputation. Moving to the Linux Foundation let companies such as Red Hat, Azure, and AWS bet on it with confidence. Burns calls the structure an insurance policy, and says it made the team more agile than startups such as Docker.
followups.speaker: Brendan Burns

blocks.speaker: Brendan Burns

blocks.question: The earliest version was you and two others hacking something together. What did the first demo do?
answer: Burns says it was almost a demo of what happens when existing open source tools are joined together. A basic control tool deployed a container across several machines. Requests to one endpoint reached different replicas, a killed instance came back, and a basic upgrade worked. Burns says that was about it.

followups.question: How long did the initial MVP take to build?
answer: Burns says a little under a week, roughly four or five days, since Burns does not work weekends.
followups.speaker: Brendan Burns

followups.question: Did you drop existing work to build it, since it was extra?
answer: Burns says the other work was not dropped outright, but there was room to slack on it for a short stretch. The MVP was hacked together with every shortcut available. Much of it came from other open source projects, joined with glue code.
followups.speaker: Brendan Burns

blocks.speaker: Brendan Burns

blocks.question: Many engineers think they cannot build something like this beside their existing responsibilities. What advice would you give?
answer: Burns gives two answers. The first is advice Burns has given everyone who worked for Burns: hide about 10 percent of your effort from management. Everyone has slack, and as an organization grows, that 10 percent can do more. Burns says many influential ideas came from it. The aim is to let people make local decisions without asking permission up the chain.

Burns warns that some ideas will fail, and the failures waste time. Still, one success may separate exceeding expectations from meeting them. A person has to accept betting on several ideas. Burns says this is not everyone's path.

Burns's second answer is that the time has to come from somewhere. Burns asks what people give up, since most have 10 to 20 hours a week outside work, spent on games, streaming, or YouTube. Burns says the returns were exponential: two times the time for a year could bring 20 times the impact.

Burns also found the work addictive. Once users filed issues on GitHub, Burns wanted to keep closing them, and kept going until falling asleep at the laptop. Burns was not thinking about a career payoff.
blocks.speaker: Brendan Burns

blocks.question: It seems it took a while to get leadership buy-in. How did that happen?
answer: Burns says it took a solid six months to go from a very hacky prototype to something a team could use. Many early hires had built similar systems, so the project felt like a clean-room chance to rebuild with better ideas. Burns says that is rare for an engineer.
There were no users yet, so the team did not have to fix bugs for a paying customer. The people involved had long thought about what the system could look like, and could now build it.
blocks.speaker: Brendan Burns

blocks.question: What does hiding 10 percent of effort from management look like in practice?
answer: Burns says a person should always have a side project that nobody assigned but that matters. The host compares this to Google's 20 percent time, and Burns agrees the idea is similar.

Burns says hide is meant literally: do not ask permission at first. A project may need a couple of months before it can be shown. Burns says a running system is far more persuasive than a document or slide deck. The manager then decides whether the built idea is good, not whether to spend time on it.

followups.question: What if nobody cares when you launch, or it is not as good as you hoped?
answer: Burns says that is the flip side. Some time will be wasted, possibly including a promotion that did not come because the work was not the breakthrough the person expected. Burns says this is a risk, like a startup. A person should enter thinking the idea is good, worth trying, and acceptable to fail.
followups.speaker: Brendan Burns

followups.question: Do senior engineers need to take that kind of risk to be promoted?
answer: The host says senior engineers who ask how to get promoted are often told to find the project, since the work has become too ambiguous to hand over. Burns agrees this becomes a necessity at higher levels, where people must come up with good ideas, not only execute them.

Burns says the project helped Burns's own career. Credit for an idea you create entirely is obvious, while credit for a bigger project or someone else's idea is harder to attribute. Burns calls it a roll of the dice, and says timing matters too.
followups.speaker: Brendan Burns

blocks.speaker: Brendan Burns

blocks.question: Borg looked like a competitive advantage for Google. How did you convince people it was acceptable to share part of it?
answer: Burns says people who leave Google are not wiped like the characters in Men in Black. The team also talked to Facebook, Twitter, and other scale-out companies building similar systems, so the technology was not really a secret. Mesos was similar, so an open source option was coming.

Burns says the team reframed the choice. The question was not whether an open source version would exist, but whether Google wanted to influence it or see someone else control it. A proprietary option was not viable.
blocks.speaker: Brendan Burns

blocks.question: With no customers yet, how did you decide the minimum feature set before launch?
answer: Burns says the team of three had complementary skills. Craig was a strong product and business lead, Joe was strong in API design, and Burns could write prototypes quickly. The team drew on the pain of deploying onto traditional infrastructure and on immutable infrastructure ideas that Netflix was discussing.
Burns says there were no customers yet, but there would be. Burns describes Kubernetes as a coalescing of ideas already circulating in the industry, given an anchor point and a clear expression.

followups.question: Did you write most of the initial code yourself?
answer: Burns estimates the high 80s percent, or more, of the original code was Burns's, though Burns is not sure of the exact figure. Burns is now about fifth on the overall GitHub commit list, after being first for a long time.
followups.speaker: Brendan Burns

blocks.speaker: Brendan Burns

blocks.question: After writing so much of the code, which part of the system was hardest to build?
answer: Burns says the hardest part was the early decision to make the system loosely coupled. Many independent control loops act across the system. That helps resiliency, but when something goes wrong, roughly 15 processes must be pieced together from many logs, and early logging and events were inconsistent.

Burns says problems that reproduce easily are simple to fix, since you add logs and run again. Transient race conditions are much harder. The team was also learning Go, with gotchas picked up on the fly.

followups.question: Was there something controlling everything, such as leader election? What did you use?
answer: Burns says the team relied almost entirely on etcd. It was an open source key-value store that CoreOS had written, now part of Kubernetes, and it implements the Raft consensus protocol. Paxos is hard to implement and not many people understand it. Raft is provably correct and much easier to implement.

Burns says etcd does not do leader election directly, but it gives enough building blocks. Burns also pushed hard for a rule that all access goes through an API server, so nothing wrote to disk directly.
followups.speaker: Brendan Burns

followups.question: What is the main benefit of routing everything through the API server?
answer: Burns says components can restart and come back working, without worrying about corruption or schema changes. Apart from etcd, they are effectively stateless, so the system was easier to make stable. The downside is loose coupling, which made debugging harder.

Burns frames it as state machines versus control loops. A state machine is easy to debug but hard to make reliable, because an unexpected state may have no clear next step. Burns says the system was designed to be stable but hard to debug. Control loops drive the current state toward a desired state, from wherever they wake up. The host recognizes this as PID control, and Burns agrees.
followups.speaker: Brendan Burns

blocks.speaker: Brendan Burns

blocks.question: Kubernetes is declarative rather than imperative. What are the pros and cons of that design?
answer: Burns says the approach was part of the wider infrastructure-as-code movement. The benefit is clarity. A list of steps records actions but not the objective, while a declaration writes down the goal, such as a reliable website, and asks the system to reach it. That record lets the system self-heal after a failure or restart.

Burns says a declaration also allows code review and unit tests. The main downside is complexity, including a YAML learning curve. Burns says there is now enough educational material, and generative AI helps. Burns's view is that the upsides are large and the downsides small.

followups.question: Does declaring the outcome also let you optimize under the hood?
answer: The host suggests so, and Burns agrees it makes machine failures easier to handle. People do not say run this on that machine. They say they want three replicas somewhere, so if a machine fails, the workload moves.
followups.speaker: Brendan Burns

blocks.speaker: Brendan Burns

blocks.question: How did you get companies such as Red Hat, with OpenShift, to bet on Kubernetes?
answer: Burns says many early partners were building a platform or a reliable web service anyway. For them, building the same layer together beat building it alone, because their value was not in that layer.

Burns says partners had to be equals. Taking a dependency also means depending on someone's roadmap, so the team offered a seat at the design table. Later, networking and storage providers joined, because their users were moving to Kubernetes.
blocks.speaker: Brendan Burns

blocks.question: How did you keep Google from dominating the roadmap, when Google started and largely funded the project?
answer: Burns says independence was critical to adoption. The first step was a foundation. About a year in, the team donated all of Kubernetes to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, under the Linux Foundation, because partners cannot easily collaborate when one company holds the trademarks.

The second step came later. The project had no written governance for its first few years, which Burns calls a mistake. In 2016 the team wrote rules so that no single company could take control, with a distributed, democratic model rather than a benevolent dictator. The host says contributors would not join without good governance, and Burns agrees.

followups.question: Do you mean a constitution? Did you write it yourselves, or did lawyers?
answer: Burns says the team wrote it. About seven or eight people met in a couple of intense sessions, looked at other communities, and codified loose arrangements that already existed informally. They also created a steering committee, which had never existed before.

Burns says the group was called the bootstrap committee. Its members were respected leaders who did not fight with each other. Burns credits Sarah Novotny, the community leader at the time, with bringing them together.
followups.speaker: Brendan Burns

blocks.speaker: Brendan Burns

blocks.question: What share of contributions comes from the community, and what share from the main companies?
answer: Burns does not have Kubernetes numbers. From general open source experience, core contributors make up roughly 80 to 90 percent of the work, and less than 10 percent comes from other people. Companies such as Microsoft commit to upstream teams, but for many users, technology is a means to an end.

Burns says it is hard to justify putting 10 percent of staff into upstream work at a bank or retailer, especially when leaders did not grow up in open source. Legal teams also block some contributions, because they fear liability for bugs. Burns says that worry does not hold water, and the Linux Foundation can supply case law, but it can still be enough to stop a contribution.

followups.question: Would someone actually be sued for adding a bug?
answer: Burns says the chain of logic is easy to imagine, such as an open source JPEG library in a smoke detector causing a fire. Burns does not think it holds, since many open source licenses include indemnification language. Burns says a developer in a non-tech company may not be able to argue with legal, so the contribution fades away.
followups.speaker: Brendan Burns

blocks.speaker: Brendan Burns

blocks.question: How has Kubernetes adjusted to AI training, which runs in huge bursts, and to inference, which needs low latency?
answer: Burns says Kubernetes could not handle much more than about 100 nodes early on. The team optimized the core systems and reduced noisy APIs. etcd can be the main bottleneck at scale, so running etcd well is central. Burns compares this to any large database: the team ran the system, saw where it broke, fixed it, and repeated.

Burns says cloud users changed the shape of demand. On AKS a cluster appears in about two minutes, so many users run hundreds or thousands of smaller clusters. The team had to invest, with Azure, in managing clusters consistently. Burns jokes that containers were meant to end snowflake servers, and now clusters are the snowflakes.

followups.question: Is there an upper bound? If load rose tenfold, would Kubernetes break?
answer: Burns says the storage layer is the limit. Most other parts scale out horizontally. At ten times the load, the team may have to make etcd scale or replace it with something similar that can run at larger scale. Burns sees nothing inherent in the design that prevents this.

Burns cites a familiar saying: every time you change an order of magnitude, the problem moves. Burns expects people to keep pushing scale, because motivation drives the work, as long as the design does not block it.
followups.speaker: Brendan Burns

blocks.speaker: Brendan Burns

blocks.question: You have a PhD in robotics, and many people advise against PhDs. What is your view?
answer: Burns says it is among the top questions Burns gets. In one story, a college classmate went into start-ups and industry, and ended up at the same level as Burns, who had done a PhD. Burns says it probably does not matter much either way.

Burns also says the PhD was fun, and taught writing and presenting ideas that industry did not. That helped in the six-month argument for open sourcing the project. Burns later taught CS 101 for a couple of years, which helped explain Kubernetes to newcomers.
Burns's summary: the degree probably does not matter, but Burns learned useful skills and had fun.

followups.question: What is the top question you get asked?
answer: Burns says the most common question is how to know what to learn. Burns does not care which field someone learns, only that they are learning. Find something you are excited about, because you will then put in the effort instead of watching YouTube. Systems engineers are still needed.

Burns says there was never a career plan. Burns chased things that seemed useful or fun. A plan suits some people, but things that look like mistakes can become critical lessons. As long as you are learning, you are probably fine.
followups.speaker: Brendan Burns

blocks.speaker: Brendan Burns

blocks.question: Burns has said the inevitable trajectory of software is death. How could Kubernetes end?
answer: Burns still stands by it. The point is not to cling to software that is dying, and to be willing to throw code away. Burns says Kubernetes's own original code has been rewritten several times. An ending would likely be something that achieves similar things more easily, with less complexity.

Burns expects some technologies to become hidden. A reliable natural-language interface could make a web service easier to request than writing YAML. Burns notes that Kubernetes sits on Linux, and Linux on a processor, and people may focus so much on AI that they forget the layers beneath.

Burns would be surprised if Kubernetes was still running in 100 years, though computing has not existed long enough to be sure. Six years ago Burns would have doubted x86 was going away on servers. Now GPUs do much of the processing, and ARM64 matters on servers for energy reasons. Burns compares predictions with self-driving cars, which were five years away for about 15 years.
blocks.speaker: Brendan Burns

blocks.question: Is there a book that most affected your career?
answer: Burns says the biggest early influence was the Gang of Four book on design patterns, from the late 1990s or mid-1990s. The host names it as Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software, and Burns agrees. Later, Leadership on the Line mattered as Burns became a large organization leader, and The Five Dysfunctions of Teams is good for how teams operate, though Burns is unsure of that title.

followups.question: So engineers should read the first book, and managers the other two?
answer: The host sums it up that way, and Burns says that is about right, though a career evolves and a person may read both.
followups.speaker: Brendan Burns

blocks.speaker: Brendan Burns

blocks.question: If you could go back to just after college and give yourself advice, what would you say?
answer: Burns says keep better notes. There is a strong MBA thesis or book in the Kubernetes journey, but Burns does not have enough notes to write it.
The host jokes that an LLM could parse the code. Burns says notes and code are not the main gap. Burns misses the partner discussions and interpersonal work, which Burns remembers only in part.
blocks.speaker: Brendan Burns
